prize_parts.citation: for their theories of how special-interest politics shapes trade policy, and of how trade, innovation and growth interact in open economies

statement.case_for: Grossman and Helpman turned trade policy from an exogenous tariff choice into an equilibrium outcome of lobbying and electoral incentives. The 'Protection for Sale' framework gives sharp, estimable predictions about which sectors get protected and how, and it has been taken to data and used in analyses of trade agreements. Their other joint work on innovation, growth and trade adds a second pillar. The attribution is clean: a stable two-person partnership with jointly authored core papers. Three decades of testing, extension and teaching remove any timing concern. This is theory built to explain observed policy patterns, which is the standard I weigh most heavily. It is also a field where the prize has not gone to a political-economy treatment of trade policy. The gap in trade-theory recognition since 2008 is a point about the field, not a reason for merit.
statement.case_against: Empirical support for the specific protection-for-sale predictions is mixed. Part of the contribution is conceptual rather than demonstrably policy-changing. Krugman's 2008 prize covered the new-trade-theory foundations, and Helpman's separate role in firm-heterogeneity work (B041) means a Helpman award could be framed in several ways. The committee may also judge that the stronger recent evidence-based programmes, such as B038 and B002, have more direct and measurable influence on policy debate. I rank the theoretical and conceptual depth of B013 above that.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B041 first. He regards Melitz's firm-heterogeneity framework, with Helpman, as the reorganising advance in modern trade theory, with over twenty years of confirmation, and he treats Helpman's work as the natural second name.
responses.response: I accept that Melitz (2003) is a major contribution and that its confirmation record is strong. I place it below B013 for two reasons. First, the Melitz-Helpman-Yeaple extensions and the quantitative strand sit close to a literature where Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made parallel contributions that this ballot does not credit, so attribution is less clean than for Grossman-Helpman. Second, Helpman can sensibly be honoured once. If the committee prefers the firm-heterogeneity framing, I would not oppose it on merit, but I think the joint Grossman-Helpman programme is the more complete body of work.

responses.point: Teorell supports B012 and would add Mark Gertler to Kiyotaki and Moore, crediting the financial-accelerator line alongside the collateral-constraint mechanism.
responses.response: I rank B012 second, so we agree on the importance of Kiyotaki-Moore. I would still keep it to the two originators. The accelerator line is a related but distinct strand (Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist), and Bernanke's 2022 prize already covered much of it. Adding Gertler would blur the attribution and make the citation less coherent. I would also note that direct identification of the collateral channel is still debated, which is part of why I place B012 behind B013.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B038 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) first. She argues it combines new data with an explanatory framework, with high societal impact and a research design that has become standard after more than fifteen years.
responses.response: I did not rank B038, and I should be clear about why. The credible local-labour-market design is a real strength. My concerns are narrower. The shift-share identification debate and the persistence of the effects are not fully settled. The task-based half of the entry draws on contributors outside the credited names. The ballot also bundles two programmes, which makes a single citation harder to write. Colleagues disagree on the third name (Dorn or Katz), which shows the attribution is not yet resolved. I take the point that its empirical quality is high and I would be comfortable with it as a strong alternative, but I do not think it displaces B013 on foundational depth.

responses.point: Krusell also ranks B013 first. He values both the protection-for-sale framework and the integration of endogenous growth with trade and technology diffusion, but he notes that Krugman 2008 may have covered part of trade theory and that Helpman's presence on B041 could favour another configuration.
responses.response: I agree with the substance and with the caveat. The Krugman overlap is real for the monopolistic-competition foundation. It is much weaker for the political-economy and growth-and-trade strands, which are what this citation rests on. I would write the citation around those strands so the prize does not appear to duplicate 2008. On the B041 overlap, I treat it as a framing question for the committee, not a merit objection. I would not let a possible later Melitz recognition count against a Grossman-Helpman award.

responses.point: Andersson ranks the Rubinstein-Wolinsky bargaining model (B001) first. He sees a foundational, fully mature result whose main risk is that recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I agree the alternating-offers model is canonical and that maturity is not in doubt, and I ranked it eighth, not lower, for that reason. My reservation is the weaker link to observed contracts and policy than for the programmes I prefer. Game theory is also well covered by earlier prizes. The remaining attribution questions about Wolinsky, Binmore and Ståhl-type precursors are less settled than for a Grossman-Helpman pair. I would not call B001 a poor candidate. I just see B013 as having broader downstream use in tested policy settings.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should give mixed empirical support for the specific protection-for-sale predictions, versus the framework's influence on how trade policy is modelled and studied.
Whether Helpman is better recognised through B013 or through the firm-heterogeneity framing in B041, and whether an award to either would foreclose the other.
Whether the 2008 trade prize reduces the committee's appetite for a second trade-theory award, even though the political-economy and growth strands are distinct.
My assessment of B012 and B030 rests on general knowledge without independent verification of the empirical record, so the ordering among my alternatives is tentative.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in corporate finance and private equity. My listed co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner, Sørensen, Robinson, Martinsson, Thomann) do not appear among the credited names on any shortlisted ballot entry. I have a long committee overlap with Hassler and Krusell, whose views I engage on merit. I am not aware of any institutional tie to the candidates.
